checks.claim: Key: Kelvin (1862, 'On the Age of the Sun's Heat', Macmillan's Magazine) argued chemical burning of the whole Sun would give only about 3,000 years' heat, i.e. fuel gone within a few thousand years
checks.note: Bahcall quotes Kelvin: 'the most energetic chemical action we know ... would only generate about 3,000 years' heat'.

checks.claim: Second source: a burning Sun could not keep its present output for more than a few thousand years
Wrong choice: the Sun holds no oxygen (false; oxygen is the third most abundant element by mass, about 0.6%; and it was not Kelvin's reason)
Wrong choices: heat cannot cross 150 million km of space; light from a fire fades before reaching Earth (both false; radiation needs no medium; neither was Kelvin's argument)
Context: Kelvin's own contraction (gravitational) age was only tens of millions of years, kept distinct from the 3,000-year chemical figure
checks.note: Grokipedia: contraction could supply the Sun's radiation for about 20 to 30 million years. In 1862 Kelvin thought 20 million years easy, 100 million most probably not reached, 500 million almost certainly not (AIP). 'Some tens of millions' is a fair summary, and the unit does not confuse the two figures.

checks.claim: Kelvin's 1862 estimates (20 million likely, not 100 million, certainly not 500 million)
'Lord Kelvin' for 1862 (he was William Thomson until 1892)
checks.note: Conventional usage, not an error.

checks.claim: Aston, weighing atoms at Cambridge (mass spectrograph, Cavendish Laboratory, 1919)
Helium atom less massive than four hydrogen atoms, about 1 part in 120 (Eddington's figure from Aston; Wikipedia: about 0.8%)
checks.note: Eddington: 'a loss of mass in the synthesis amounting to about 1 part in 120'. The context's modern ~0.7% is consistent (old vs modern measures).

checks.claim: Eddington's address at Cardiff, August 1920 (24 August 1920, British Association)
Eddington rejected contraction as too short-lived
checks.note: 'Lord Kelvin's date of the creation of the sun is treated with no more respect than Archbishop Ussher's.'

checks.claim: Key: stars shine by building helium out of hydrogen
Wrong choices: breaking helium into hydrogen (takes energy in), burning hydrogen with oxygen (chemical), radium decay (a 1903 suggestion, not Eddington's)
Context: ~0.7% of mass to energy; ~600 million tonnes of hydrogen fused per second; ~4 million tonnes of mass to energy per second
checks.note: Roughly 600 million tonnes per second; 3.86e26 W / c^2 is about 4.3 million tonnes per second.

checks.claim: Context: radium put forward as the Sun's fuel in 1903
checks.note: W. E. Wilson, Nature, July 1903.

checks.claim: Coulomb barrier ~0.5 MeV vs typical thermal energy ~1 keV in the core: hundreds of times too little
Eddington 'told them to go and find a hotter place' (paraphrase, not in quotation marks)
checks.note: The Internal Constitution of the Stars (1926): 'We do not argue with the critic who urges that the stars are not hot enough for this process; we tell him to go and find a hotter place.' Correctly framed as his reply to critics who said the stars were too cool.

checks.claim: Key: tunnelling; a few nuclei get through a barrier they cannot climb
Gamow 1928 (alpha decay); Atkinson and Houtermans 1929 applied it to fusion in stars, assuming 40 million degrees
checks.note: Atkinson and Houtermans, Z. Physik 54 (1929), assumed 40 million degrees and a density of ~10 g/cm3.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: better measures showed the core far hotter (false; ~15 million C, cooler than the 40 million assumed)
Wrong choices: weight forces nuclei into contact; nuclei lose their charge (both false); core ~150 times the density of water
checks.note: Central density 150 g/cm3.

checks.claim: Bethe worked out the Sun's reactions in 1938 (with Critchfield, after the Washington conference) and 1939 (CNO cycle paper)
Homestake: 615 tonnes of perchloroethylene (chlorine-rich cleaning fluid), 1,478 m down a gold mine at Lead, South Dakota
Davis found about a third of the predicted flux (2.56 SNU vs ~7.5 SNU)
Key: SNO (Canada) 2001 found most of them change into kinds chlorine cannot catch (chlorine sees electron neutrinos only)
checks.note: First results 18 June 2001 gave the first direct evidence that solar neutrinos change kind. About 34-35% arrive as electron neutrinos.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: neutrino decay, a cooler core, Davis's count wrong (all proposed, all ruled out)
Context: SNO 2,100 m down a nickel mine in Ontario (Creighton), 1,000 tonnes of heavy water; total matched models; neutrinos have mass
checks.note: Nuance only: the 2001 total came from SNO's electron count set against Super-Kamiokande; SNO's own count of all kinds (neutral current) was published in 2002. Wikipedia states the 2001 total agreed with theory, so the context passes.

checks.claim: Nobels: Bethe 1967; Davis a share of 2002; McDonald a share of 2015 (with Kajita)
checks.note: 2002: half to Davis and Koshiba jointly, half to Giacconi; 'a share' is right. 2015: Kajita and McDonald (APS News 2015/11).

checks.claim: Light crosses from the surface to Earth in about 8 minutes (about 8 min 20 s, 150 million km)
The trip out is from about 10,000 to well over 100,000 years by most estimates
checks.note: Shu: of order 10,000 years; Mitalas and Sills's model: 170,000 years (NASA's figure); other estimates 20,000-200,000. The stated range is honest, and the unit says it is an estimate.

checks.claim: NASA: about 170,000 years from core to top of the convection zone; Grokipedia: 170,000 years to cross the radiative zone
Key: light is absorbed and re-emitted in random directions (random walk)
Wrong choices: conduction, gravity pulling light back, energy waiting in the core (all false)
Context: convection carries it through the outer third much faster; neutrinos cross the Sun in about 2 seconds
checks.note: R_Sun / c is about 2.3 s.

checks.claim: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and roughly halfway through its main-sequence life
checks.note: Grokipedia: about 4.6 billion, from radiometric dating of meteorites; total main-sequence life about 10 billion years. NASA rounds to 4.5 billion.

checks.claim: Key and context: 'the oldest grains in meteorites' date to about 4.57 billion years and give the Sun's age
checks.note: The oldest grains in meteorites are presolar grains, stardust from older stars, which predate the Sun by up to about 3 billion years (Murchison grains, Heck et al. 2020: https://eos.org/articles/dust-older-than-the-sun-sheds-light-on-galactic-history). The Sun's age comes from the oldest solids FORMED in the Solar System, the calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions (4,567-4,568 million years; Wikipedia says these are the oldest dated solids 'apart from presolar grains'). Fix the key to 'Dating the first solids of the Solar System, kept in meteorites' and the context's first sentence to 'The first solids to form around the young Sun, grains rich in calcium and aluminium found in some meteorites, date by their radioactive elements to about 4.57 billion years, and the Sun's age is taken from them.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Earth's oldest rocks (about 4.03 billion, Acasta Gneiss; crust remade by plate tectonics)
Wrong choices: timing the Sun's shrinking or cooling and counting back (not how the age is found)
Context: about half the hydrogen at the very centre used up (about 71% to 33-34% by mass)
Context: the Sun 'should go on shining much as it does now for about 5 billion years more'
checks.note: About 5 billion years more of hydrogen fusion in the core is right (NASA), but the Sun brightens about 10% each billion years and is about twice as bright by the end of that stage, so 'much as it does now' overstates the steadiness. Suggested: 'which should go on fusing hydrogen in its core, slowly growing brighter, for about 5 billion years more.'

checks.claim: A lone sunspot would shine brighter than the full Moon; still thousands of degrees hot (umbra about 3,000-4,500 K)
checks.note: 'a single sunspot would shine brighter than the full moon, with a crimson-orange color'.

checks.claim: Key: cooler because strong magnetic fields hold back the convective transport of heat
Context: fields thousands of times stronger than the quiet Sun's (2,000-4,000 G vs about 1 G)
Context: umbra some 1,500 degrees or more cooler than a surface of about 5,500 C (5,772 K)
checks.note: Umbra 3,000-4,500 K vs 5,772 K: 1,300-2,800 K cooler; 'some 1,500 or more' is a fair summary.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: fusion beneath died down (fusion only in core), dark cloud, shadow of small moons (all false)
Context: Scheiner took them for clusters of small moons; Galileo (Letters on Sunspots, 1613) showed they lie on the Sun's face and turn with it
Schwabe, pharmacist of Dessau, observed every clear day 1826-1843, seeking a planet inside Mercury's orbit
checks.note: He trained in and ran the family pharmacy (sold 1829); 'a pharmacist' is fair.

checks.claim: Key: sunspot numbers rose and fell over about ten years ('a probable ten-year period')
Context: reported in 1843
checks.note: 'Sonnenbeobachtungen im Jahre 1843' was written on 31 Dec 1843 and printed in Astronomische Nachrichten 21 (1844); '1843' is the usual date.

checks.claim: Context: little notice at first; Rudolf Wolf took up regular counts; RAS Gold Medal 1857
Context: cycle averages about 11 years, from just under 10 to just over 12; magnetic poles swap about every 11 years; flares most often near maximum
checks.note: NASA: the poles change magnetic polarity about every 11 years. Grokipedia Solar flare: most common at solar maximum.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: steady growth over seventeen years (1826-1843 = 17 years), no change, seasonal (all false)
Carrington, drawing sunspots in England just before noon on 1 September 1859, saw two patches of intensely bright white light that faded within five minutes
checks.note: Carrington: 'two patches of intensely bright and white light broke out' ... 'In this lapse of 5 minutes'. Grokipedia: about 11:18 a.m.

checks.claim: About 17 hours later (17.6 h); auroras as far south as Cuba
Telegraph sparks across Europe and North America; operators shocked; paper set alight
One line (Boston-Portland) disconnected batteries and sent messages for about two hours
Key: the changing geomagnetic field drove the current (geomagnetically induced current); wrong choices (particles falling on wires, leftover battery charge, lightning) false
Quote: Carrington wrote 'one swallow does not make a summer'
checks.note: Wikipedia and the National Academies' Storms from the Sun both attribute it to his report; the arXiv paper on his legacy takes it as its title.

checks.claim: Context: flares release magnetic energy near sunspots; March 1989 storm blacked out Quebec for up to nine hours
B2FH 1957: Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler, Fred Hoyle; stars forge elements in their lives (s-process) and in supernovae (r-process)
Dying stars scatter their elements into space, seeding new stars and planets
Key: the hydrogen in the body's water came from the Big Bang, not stars
checks.note: NASA APOD: the hydrogen in your body and in every water molecule came from the Big Bang; no other appreciable source. The unit does not claim hydrogen is the only exception (trace boron, for instance, is from cosmic rays), so the stem stands.

checks.claim: Big Bang made hydrogen, helium and a little lithium
checks.note: The Big Bang made most of the helium; stars have since added some. The context's 'with helium' is fair.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: oxygen in water and carbon made by fusion in stars; much iron made in supernovae
Context: hydrogen is about a tenth of body mass and about six of every ten atoms
checks.note: 9.5% by mass, 62% of atoms.

unit_notes: 9 ok, 1 error (5ebe7acfdb, the oldest meteorite grains are presolar stardust, older than the Sun; the Sun's age comes from the first solids formed in the Solar System, the CAIs). The same question also has an uncertain context line ('shining much as it does now' for 5 billion years; the Sun brightens about 10% a billion years). Fact-sheet slip that did not reach the questions: F16 says Davis won half of the 2002 Nobel; he and Koshiba shared one half, with the other half to Giacconi (the question's 'a share' is right). Optional polish for dad75b7a60: SNO's own count of every kind was published in 2002, and the 2001 total came from its count set against Super-Kamiokande's.
